newsitem.title: MEXICO: Death toll rises to four as Mexico fire snuffed out.
newsitem.headline: Death toll rises to four as Mexico fire snuffed out.

text.p: Firefighters on Wednesday finally snuffed out a blaze in three huge fuel tanks two days after they exploded outside Mexico City, killing four people, officials said.

Live television pictures on Wednesday showed the blackened ruins of the three tanks, where more than 100,000 barrels of fuel went up in flames. The installation was the site 12 years ago of a series of natural gas tank explosions that killed 511 people and destroyed homes over a wide area.
At least 16 people were injured in the disaster, which sent huge clouds of black smoke billowing three miles (five km) into the sky.

As more than 5,000 evacuees from the northern suburb of San Juan Ixhuatepec returned to their homes, Mexican opposition congressmen demanded the resignation of the head of the state oil monopoly, Pemex, owner of the installation.
Pemex has had a string of fatal disasters in recent years, including a 1992 leak that blew up whole streets and killed more than 200 people in Mexico's second city, Guadalajara.

Pemex Chairman Adrian Lajous "must leave Pemex," left-wing Senator Felix Salgado Macedonio said. "It is not right that he is still being kept in that job; ineptitude, incompetence and corruption is rampant in Pemex," he said.

"If my resignation would serve to improve the operating efficiency of Pemex or would serve to improve the security of our installations, I would seriously consider that possibility. I don't believe it would. I will stay at the head of this company," Lajous told a news conference.

Pemex said a fireman and a Pemex worker died in a hospital of their burns on Tuesday and two more victims died of their burns early on Wednesday. The blast occurred when Pemex workers were repairing a valve in a tank containing 80,000 barrels of fuel at a storage facility but the exact cause was not known, Lajous said.

In Buenos Aires, Nexican President Ernesto Zedillo said he was calling for increased safety measures at oil installations following the disaster. "We are calling on specialists to give recommendations to boost safety measures and reduce (the possibility of accidents) to practically zero," he said.
